title: Access Control Models
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Access Control Models.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Access Control Models and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Access Control Models, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 8: Authorization and Access Control. It builds practical understanding of Access Control Models with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Access Control Models protects identity and data boundaries. A control that exists only in the interface can be bypassed, so policy must be enforced at the authoritative server boundary. Enforce server-side authorization for every resource operation using the authenticated principal and the resource’s verified ownership or policy; hiding a button is not an access control.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Access Control Models can be understood through this sequence: Identify caller → Resolve resource → Enforce server policy → Test allow + deny. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 55.1 Role-based access control (RBAC); 55.2 Attribute-based access control (ABAC); 55.3 Ownership-based access control; 55.4 Relationship-based permissions; 55.5 Policy evaluation and enforcement points. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Enforce server-side authorization for every resource operation using the authenticated principal and the resource’s verified ownership or policy; hiding a button is not an access control.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Access Control Models
content_blocks.expected_output: The function returns True only for a matching owner or an administrator role, assuming the identity and record came from trusted server-side lookups.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Illustrative policy function; adapt roles and object model, authenticate the caller, and test denied as well as allowed paths.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Enforce server-side authorization for every resource operation using the authenticated principal and the resource’s verified ownership or policy; hiding a button is not an access control. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Access Control Models”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Access Control Models in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Access Control Models is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Enforce server-side authorization for every resource operation using the authenticated principal and the resource’s verified ownership or policy; hiding a button is not an access control.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
